Abstract.

In this paper, we investigate the expansion of the integral form Macdonald polynomials Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) in the elementary symmetric function basis. Motivated by the connection between chromatic symmetric functions and LLT polynomials, we conjecture the ee-positivity of a normalization of Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t). We verify the conjecture when μ\mu is either a hook or a two-column partition. In the hook case, we express the ee-coefficients as weighted sums over compositions. In the two-column case, we derive explicit formulas for the ee-coefficients.

Key words and phrases: 
integral form Macdonald polynomials, ee-positivity, chromatic symmetric functions
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 05E05; Secondary: 05A30, 33D15

1. Introduction

Macdonald polynomials Pμ​(x,q,t)P_{\mu}(x;q,t) are a family of symmetric functions introduced by Macdonald in 19881988 [14, 15]. Macdonald polynomials generalize many well-known bases of symmetric functions, including Schur functions and Hall–Littlewood polynomials. Moreover, due to their deep connections with various areas such as special function theory, representation theory, algebraic geometry, and quantum mechanics, they have been the subject of extensive study since their introduction. In the same work, Macdonald also defined the integral form Macdonald polynomials Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) with coefficients in ℤ⁡[q,t]\mathbb{Z}[q,t]:

(1.1) Jμ​(x,q,t)=Pμ​(x,q,t)​∏c∈μ(1−qarm⁡(c)​tleg⁡(c)+1).J_{\mu}(x;q,t)=P_{\mu}(x;q,t)\prod_{c\in\mu}(1-q^{\operatorname{arm}(c)}t^{\operatorname{leg}(c)+1}).

See Section 2 for the precise definitions.

In 20052005, Haglund, Haiman, and Loehr [8] made a major breakthrough in Macdonald theory by discovering a combinatorial formula for the modified Macdonald polynomials H~μ​(x,q,t)\tilde{H}_{\mu}(x;q,t), defined by

(1.2) H~μ​(x,q,t)=tn⁡(μ)​Jμ​[X1−1/t;q,1/t],\tilde{H}_{\mu}(x;q,t)=t^{n(\mu)}J_{\mu}\left[\frac{X}{1-1/t};q,1/t\right],

where X=x1+x2+⋯X=x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots, the square brackets indicate plethystic substitution, and n⁡(μ)=∑i≥1(i−1)​μin(\mu)=\sum_{i\geq 1}(i-1)\mu_{i}. Haiman [11] proved that H~μ​(x,q,t)\tilde{H}_{\mu}(x;q,t) is Schur positive, i.e., its Schur coefficients belong to ℤ≥0​[q,t]\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}[q,t].

In [8], Haglund, Haiman, and Loehr expressed H~μ​(x,q,t)\tilde{H}_{\mu}(x;q,t) as a positive linear combination of LLT\operatorname{LLT} polynomials. Introduced by Lascoux, Leclerc, and Thibon [13], the LLT\operatorname{LLT} polynomials LLTν⁡(x,q)\operatorname{LLT}_{\nu}(x;q) are symmetric functions that are known to be Schur positive [6]. In general, LLT polynomials are indexed by tuples of skew shapes. The special case in which each skew shape consists of a single cell gives rise to the so-called unicellular LLT polynomials, which can also be indexed by Dyck paths.

The unicellular LLT polynomials are closely related to the chromatic symmetric functions χγ​(x,q)\chi_{\gamma}(x;q) introduced in [17] when γ\gamma is a Dyck path of length 2​n2n corresponding to the incomparability graph of a natural unit interval order. More precisely, Haglund and Wilson [10, Eq. (6)] observed that the result of Carlsson and Mellit [3, Proposition 3.5] is equivalent to

(1.3) χγ​(x,q)=LLTγ⁡[(q−1)​X;q](q−1)n.\chi_{\gamma}(x;q)=\frac{\operatorname{LLT}_{\gamma}[(q-1)X;q]}{(q-1)^{n}}.

The chromatic symmetric functions χγ​(x,q)\chi_{\gamma}(x;q) have been shown to expand positively in the elementary symmetric function basis (a property we refer to as ee-positivity henceforth) when q=1q=1 [12, 5], and were conjectured by Shareshian and Wachs [17] to have ee-coefficients in ℤ≥0​[q]\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}[q].11 1 OpenAI [16] has claimed a proof of this conjecture.

We note that (1.2) is equivalent to

(1.4) Jμ(x;q,t−1)=t−∑i≥1iμiH~μ[(t−1)X;q,t].J_{\mu}\big(x;q,t^{-1}\big)=t^{-\sum_{i\geq 1}i\mu_{i}}\,\tilde{H}_{\mu}\big[(t-1)X;q,t\big].

The present work is motivated by the analogy between (1.3) and (1.4). On the right-hand sides, the unicellular LLT polynomials LLTγ⁡(x,q)\operatorname{LLT}_{\gamma}(x;q) and the modified Macdonald polynomials H~μ​(x,q,t)\tilde{H}_{\mu}(x;q,t) are both Schur positive. In view of this, the conjectured ee-positivity of χγ​(x,q)\chi_{\gamma}(x;q) motivates the investigation of ee-positivity for suitably normalized specializations of integral form Macdonald polynomials Jμ​(x,q,t−1)J_{\mu}\big(x;q,t^{-1}\big).

With regard to Schur positivity, Haglund conjectured (see [1, Eq. (1)]) that, for every partition μ\mu and every positive integer kk, the symmetric function

Jμ​(x,q,qk)(1−q)|μ|\frac{J_{\mu}(x;q,q^{k})}{(1-q)^{|\mu|}}

has Schur coefficients in ℤ≥0​[q]\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}[q]. Several special cases have been proved in [2, 21, 22]. Furthermore, Wilson [20] conjectured that, for every negative integer kk, the expression obtained by replacing (1−q)(1-q) with (q−1)(q-1) and multiplying by a suitable power of qq is also Schur positive.

Building on this conjecture and the preceding discussion of the ee-positivity of Jμ​(x,q,t−1)J_{\mu}\big(x;q,t^{-1}\big) under an appropriate normalization, we propose the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.1.

For any partition μ\mu and any positive integer kk, the following is ee-positive:

(1.5) qk​∑i≥1i​μi​Jμ​(x,q,q−k)(q−1)|μ|.q^{k\sum_{i\geq 1}i\mu_{i}}\frac{J_{\mu}(x;q,q^{-k})}{(q-1)^{|\mu|}}.

In this paper, we prove this conjecture when μ\mu is either a hook or a two-column partition. To do this, we first consider the ee-expansion of the integral form Macdonald polynomial:

Jμ​(x,q,t)=∑λ⊢|μ|cμ,λ​(q,t)​eλ.J_{\mu}(x;q,t)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash|\mu|}c_{\mu,\lambda}(q,t)e_{\lambda}.

When μ\mu is a hook, we express the coefficients cμ,λ​(q,t)=cμ,λc_{\mu,\lambda}(q,t)=c_{\mu,\lambda} as weighted sums over compositions (Theorem 4.2). As a consequence, we obtain a positive ee-expansion of (1.5) (Corollary 4.6). When μ\mu has at most two columns, we compute the coefficients explicitly as products (Theorem 5.1), which implies the ee-positivity of (1.5). In addition, for an arbitrary partition μ\mu of nn, we give a product formula for the coefficient cμ,(n)c_{\mu,(n)} of ene_{n} (Theorem 6.1).

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we recall basic definitions and known results. In Section 3 we give an ee-expansion formula for Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) when μ\mu is a one-row partition. In Section 4 we extend this result to hooks and prove Conjecture 1.1 in this case. Section 5 treats the two-column case, and Section 6 the ene_{n}-coefficient. Finally, in Section 7, we explain a connection to α\alpha-chromatic symmetric functions and propose a conjecture on the q→1q\to 1 limit of (1.5).

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the basic definitions and known results that will be used throughout the paper.

2.1. Basic definitions

A composition of nn is a sequence α=(α1,α2,…,αl)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\dots,\alpha_{l}) of positive integers satisfying ∑iαi=n\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}=n, denoted by α⊨n\alpha\vDash n. Each αi\alpha_{i} is called a part of α\alpha, and the number of parts is called the length of α\alpha, denoted by ℓ⁡(α)\ell(\alpha). The sum of the parts of α\alpha, denoted by |α||\alpha|, is called the size of α\alpha. A partition is a composition such that the parts are weakly decreasing. If ∑iλi=n\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}=n, we say that λ\lambda is a partition of nn and write λ⊢n\lambda\vdash n. For notational convenience, we also write (0)(0) for the empty partition ∅\emptyset.

If a composition α\alpha is equal to a rearrangement of a partition λ\lambda, we write α∼λ\alpha\sim\lambda. For partitions λ,μ⊢n\lambda,\mu\vdash n, we define the dominance order by μ≤λ\mu\leq\lambda if

μ1+⋯+μi≤λ1+⋯+λi for all ​i≥1,\mu_{1}+\cdots+\mu_{i}\leq\lambda_{1}+\cdots+\lambda_{i}\quad\text{ for all }i\geq 1,

where both partitions are extended by zeros. We also write (0)(0) for the empty composition ∅\emptyset

Given a partition λ=(λ1,…,λk)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{k}), its diagram is an array of unit squares, called cells, with λi\lambda_{i} cells in the iith row from the bottom, left-justified. We often identify λ\lambda with its diagram. A cell in row ii and column jj is denoted by (i,j)(i,j). The conjugate λ′\lambda^{\prime} of λ\lambda is the partition whose diagram is obtained from λ\lambda by reflecting across the diagonal y=xy=x. The reading order of λ\lambda is the order of its cells obtained by reading the rows from top to bottom and the cells in each row from left to right.

A partition of the form (r,1s)(r,1^{s}) with r≥1r\geq 1 and s≥0s\geq 0 is called a hook. Here, aba^{b} means the sequence of bb aa’s. Note that hooks include one-row partitions (n)(n) and one-column partitions (1n)=(1,1n−1)(1^{n})=(1,1^{n-1}).

Given a cell c∈λc\in\lambda, the arm (resp. coarm) length of c=(i,j)c=(i,j) is the number of cells in row ii to the right (resp. left) of cc in λ\lambda, denoted by arm⁡(c)\operatorname{arm}(c) (resp. arm′⁡(c)\operatorname{arm}^{\prime}(c)). The leg (resp. coleg) length of c=(i,j)c=(i,j) is the number of cells in column jj strictly above (resp. below) cc in λ\lambda, denoted by leg⁡(c)\operatorname{leg}(c) (resp. leg′⁡(c)\operatorname{leg}^{\prime}(c)). See Figure 1 for an example.

For a partition λ\lambda, a semistandard Young tableau of shape λ\lambda is a filling of λ\lambda with positive integers such that the entries are weakly increasing from left to right in each row and strictly increasing from bottom to top in each column. We use SSYT⁡(λ)\operatorname{SSYT}(\lambda) to denote the set of semistandard Young tableaux of shape λ\lambda.

For a nonnegative integer rr and a partition μ\mu, we use the qq-Pochhammer symbols

(a,q)r=∏i=0r−1(1−a​qi),(a,q)μ=∏i=1ℓ⁡(μ)(a,q)μi,(a;q)_{r}=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(1-aq^{i}),\qquad(a;q)_{\mu}=\prod_{i=1}^{\ell(\mu)}(a;q)_{\mu_{i}},

where (a,q)0=1(a;q)_{0}=1. For integers n,kn,k with 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n, the qq-binomial coefficient is defined by

[nk]q=(q,q)n(q,q)k​(q,q)n−k.\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{k}_{q}=\frac{(q;q)_{n}}{(q;q)_{k}(q;q)_{n-k}}.

We also define

[n]q=1+q+⋯+qn−1,[n]q!=∏i=1n[i]q.[n]_{q}=1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1},\qquad[n]_{q}!=\prod_{i=1}^{n}[i]_{q}.

For a partition λ=(λ1,…,λl)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{l}), the monomial symmetric function mλm_{\lambda} is defined by mλ=∑xα,m_{\lambda}=\sum x^{\alpha}, where the sum is over all sequences α=(α1,α2,…)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\dots) obtained by rearranging (λ1,…,λl,0,0,…)(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{l},0,0,\dots), and xα=x1α1x2α2⋯x^{\alpha}=x_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}x_{2}^{\alpha_{2}}\cdots. The elementary symmetric function eλe_{\lambda} is defined by eλ=∏ieλie_{\lambda}=\prod_{i}e_{\lambda_{i}}, where en=∑i1<⋯<inxi1⋯xine_{n}=\sum_{i_{1}<\cdots<i_{n}}x_{i_{1}}\cdots x_{i_{n}}. The complete homogeneous symmetric function hλh_{\lambda} is defined by hλ=∏ihλih_{\lambda}=\prod_{i}h_{\lambda_{i}}, where hn=∑i1≤⋯≤inxi1⋯xinh_{n}=\sum_{i_{1}\leq\cdots\leq i_{n}}x_{i_{1}}\cdots x_{i_{n}}. sλ=∑T∈SSYT⁡(λ)xT,s_{\lambda}=\sum_{T\in\operatorname{SSYT}(\lambda)}x^{T},

where xT=∏ixiaix^{T}=\prod_{i}x_{i}^{a_{i}} with aia_{i} the number of occurrences of ii in TT.

We note that each of {mλ}\{m_{\lambda}\}, {eλ}\{e_{\lambda}\}, {hλ}\{h_{\lambda}\}, {pλ}\{p_{\lambda}\}, and {sλ}\{s_{\lambda}\} forms a basis of the space of symmetric functions. With a slight abuse of notation, for any of the bases {gλ}\{g_{\lambda}\} listed above, we write [gλ]​f[g_{\lambda}]f for the coefficient of gλg_{\lambda} in the expansion of a symmetric function f∈ΛFf\in\Lambda_{F} in that basis.

Let E=E⁡(t1,t2,…)E=E(t_{1},t_{2},\dots) be a formal Laurent series in t1,t2,…t_{1},t_{2},\dots with rational coefficients. For f=∑λcλ​pλ∈ΛFf=\sum_{\lambda}c_{\lambda}p_{\lambda}\in\Lambda_{F}, the plethystic substitution f⁡[E]f[E] is defined by

f⁡[E]:=∑λcλ​pλ​[E],f[E]:=\sum_{\lambda}c_{\lambda}p_{\lambda}[E],

where pλ​[E]=∏ipλi​[E]p_{\lambda}[E]=\prod_{i}p_{\lambda_{i}}[E] and pk​[E]=E⁡(t1k,t2k,…)p_{k}[E]=E\left(t_{1}^{k},t_{2}^{k},\dots\right). We refer the reader to [15, Ch. I, §8] for more details on plethysm.

2.3. Macdonald polynomials

The Macdonald polynomials Pμ=Pμ​(x,q,t)P_{\mu}=P_{\mu}(x;q,t) are the unique symmetric functions satisfying

Pμ=mμ+∑λ<μuμ​λ​(q,t)​mλ,⟨Pλ,Pμ⟩q,t=0if ​λ≠μ,P_{\mu}=m_{\mu}+\sum_{\lambda<\mu}u_{\mu\lambda}(q,t)m_{\lambda},\qquad\langle P_{\lambda},P_{\mu}\rangle_{q,t}=0\quad\text{if }\lambda\neq\mu,

for suitable coefficients uμ​λ​(q,t)∈Fu_{\mu\lambda}(q,t)\in F; see [14, 15]. Here, ⟨⋅,⋅⟩q,t\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{q,t} is the inner product on ΛF\Lambda_{F} determined by

(2.1) ⟨pλ,pμ⟩q,t=δλ​μ​zλ​∏i=1ℓ⁡(λ)1−qλi1−tλi,zλ=∏r≥1rmr​(λ)​mr​(λ)!,\langle p_{\lambda},p_{\mu}\rangle_{q,t}=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_{\lambda}\prod_{i=1}^{\ell(\lambda)}\frac{1-q^{\lambda_{i}}}{1-t^{\lambda_{i}}},\qquad z_{\lambda}=\prod_{r\geq 1}r^{m_{r}(\lambda)}m_{r}(\lambda)!,

where mr​(λ)m_{r}(\lambda) is the multiplicity of rr in λ\lambda. The integral form Macdonald polynomials Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) and the modified Macdonald polynomials H~μ​(x,q,t)\tilde{H}_{\mu}(x;q,t) are defined by

Jμ​(x,q,t)\displaystyle J_{\mu}(x;q,t) =Pμ​(x,q,t)​∏c∈μ(1−qarm⁡(c)​tleg⁡(c)+1),\displaystyle=P_{\mu}(x;q,t)\prod_{c\in\mu}(1-q^{\operatorname{arm}(c)}t^{\operatorname{leg}(c)+1}),
(2.2) H~μ​[X;q,t]\displaystyle\tilde{H}_{\mu}[X;q,t] =tn⁡(μ)​Jμ​[X1−t−1;q,t−1],\displaystyle=t^{n(\mu)}J_{\mu}\left[\frac{X}{1-t^{-1}};q,t^{-1}\right],

where n⁡(μ)=∑i(i−1)​μin(\mu)=\sum_{i}(i-1)\mu_{i}. In [8], Haglund, Haiman, and Loehr discovered a remarkable combinatorial formula for H~μ​(x,q,t)\tilde{H}_{\mu}(x;q,t). To state their result, we need some definitions.

For a partition μ⊢n\mu\vdash n, a filling σ:μ→ℤ+\sigma:\mu\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{+} is an assignment of positive integers to the cells in the diagram of μ\mu. A filling is standard if the entries are precisely 1,2,…,|μ|1,2,\dots,|\mu|. The monomial xσx^{\sigma} associated with the filling σ\sigma is defined by

xσ=∏c∈μxσ⁡(c).x^{\sigma}=\prod_{c\in\mu}x_{\sigma(c)}.

For a cell c=(i,j)∈μc=(i,j)\in\mu, let South⁡(i,j)=(i−1,j)\operatorname{South}(i,j)=(i-1,j). Given a filling σ:μ→ℤ+\sigma:\mu\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{+}, the descent set Des⁡(σ)\operatorname{Des}(\sigma) and the major index maj⁡(σ)\operatorname{maj}(\sigma) are defined by

Des⁡(σ)\displaystyle\operatorname{Des}(\sigma) ={c∈μ:South(c)∈μ,σ(c)>σ(South(c))},\displaystyle=\{c\in\mu:\operatorname{South}(c)\in\mu,\,\sigma(c)>\sigma(\operatorname{South}(c))\},
maj⁡(σ)\displaystyle\operatorname{maj}(\sigma) =∑c∈Des⁡(σ)(leg⁡(c)+1).\displaystyle=\sum_{c\in\operatorname{Des}(\sigma)}(\operatorname{leg}(c)+1).

A triple of μ\mu is a set {u,v,w}\{u,v,w\} of three cells with u,v∈μu,v\in\mu such that vv is in the same row as uu and strictly to its right, and w=South⁡(u)w=\operatorname{South}(u), which may be below the first row. Let σ\sigma be a filling of μ\mu. We orient a triple by starting at the cell whose entry is smallest, proceeding to the cell with the next-largest entry, and ending at the cell with the largest entry. If two cells have the same entry, the entry of the cell that appears earlier in the reading order of μ\mu is considered smaller. The triple is an inversion triple if this circular motion is counterclockwise, and a coinversion triple if it is clockwise. We denote by inv⁡(σ)\operatorname{inv}(\sigma) (resp. coinv⁡(σ)\operatorname{coinv}(\sigma)) the number of inversion triples (resp. coinversion triples) of σ\sigma. Here, we define σ⁡(w)=∞\sigma(w)=\infty if ww is below the first row. Note that

coinv⁡(σ)=n⁡(μ′)−inv⁡(σ).\operatorname{coinv}(\sigma)=n(\mu^{\prime})-\operatorname{inv}(\sigma).
Theorem 2.1 ([8, Theorem 2.2]).

For a partition μ\mu, the modified Macdonald polynomial H~μ​(x,q,t)\tilde{H}_{\mu}(x;q,t) is given by

(2.3) H~μ(x;q,t)=∑σ:μ→ℤ+xσqinv⁡(σ)tmaj⁡(σ).\tilde{H}_{\mu}(x;q,t)=\sum_{\sigma:\mu\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{+}}x^{\sigma}q^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)}t^{\operatorname{maj}(\sigma)}.

By (2.2), we have

(2.4) Jμ​(x,q,t)=tn⁡(μ)​H~μ​[X⁡(1−t);q,t−1]=tn⁡(μ)+n​H~μ′​[X⁡(t−1−1);t−1,q].J_{\mu}(x;q,t)=t^{n(\mu)}\tilde{H}_{\mu}[X(1-t);q,t^{-1}]=t^{n(\mu)+n}\tilde{H}_{\mu^{\prime}}[X(t^{-1}-1);t^{-1},q].

To state a combinatorial interpretation for Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t), we introduce the necessary definitions.

We say that a cell u∈μu\in\mu attacks the cells in the same row and strictly to its right, and the cells in the row below and strictly to its left. A filling σ:μ→ℤ+\sigma:\mu\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{+} is nonattacking if there are no cells u,v∈μu,v\in\mu such that uu attacks vv and σ⁡(u)=σ⁡(v)\sigma(u)=\sigma(v).

Let 𝒜+={1,2,…}\mathcal{A}_{+}=\{1,2,\dots\}, 𝒜−={1¯,2¯,…}\mathcal{A}_{-}=\{\overline{1},\overline{2},\dots\}, and 𝒜±=𝒜+∪𝒜−\mathcal{A}_{\pm}=\mathcal{A}_{+}\cup\mathcal{A}_{-}. We write |i|=i|i|=i and |i¯|=i|\overline{i}|=i. A superfilling is an assignment σ:μ→𝒜±\sigma:\mu\rightarrow\mathcal{A}_{\pm} of elements in 𝒜±\mathcal{A}_{\pm} to the cells in μ\mu. We denote by |σ||\sigma| the filling obtained from σ\sigma by replacing each entry i¯\overline{i} with ii. We say that a superfilling σ\sigma is nonattacking if |σ||\sigma| is nonattacking. We denote by neg⁡(σ)\operatorname{neg}(\sigma) the number of entries of σ\sigma in 𝒜−\mathcal{A}_{-}. Let NASF⁡(μ)\operatorname{NASF}(\mu) denote the set of nonattacking superfillings of μ\mu.

Given a total order ≺\prec on 𝒜±\mathcal{A}_{\pm}, the standardization of σ\sigma with respect to ≺\prec is the bijective filling σ≺st:μ→{1,…,n}\sigma^{\mathrm{st}}_{\prec}:\mu\to\{1,\dots,n\} obtained by relabeling the cells in increasing order of their entries, where ties between cells holding the same letter are broken by reading order: a letter in 𝒜+\mathcal{A}_{+} read earlier is regarded as smaller, and a letter in 𝒜−\mathcal{A}_{-} read earlier is regarded as larger.

Haglund, Haiman, and Loehr [8, Eq. (63)] found a combinatorial interpretation for Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t). We will use the following reformulation from [7, (A.30)].

Theorem 2.2.

We have

(2.5) Jμ​(x,q,t)=∑σ∈NASF⁡(μ′)x|σ|​qmaj⁡(σ)​tcoinv⁡(σ)​(−t)neg⁡(σ),J_{\mu}(x;q,t)=\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{NASF}(\mu^{\prime})}x^{|\sigma|}q^{\operatorname{maj}(\sigma)}t^{\operatorname{coinv}(\sigma)}(-t)^{\operatorname{neg}(\sigma)},

where maj⁡(σ)=maj⁡(σ≺st)\operatorname{maj}(\sigma)=\operatorname{maj}(\sigma^{\mathrm{st}}_{\prec}) and coinv⁡(σ)=coinv⁡(σ≺st)\operatorname{coinv}(\sigma)=\operatorname{coinv}(\sigma^{\mathrm{st}}_{\prec}), with standardization taken with respect to the ordering

(2.6) 1≺1¯≺2≺2¯≺⋯≺n≺n¯≺⋯.1\prec\overline{1}\prec 2\prec\overline{2}\prec\cdots\prec n\prec\overline{n}\prec\cdots.

3. One-row case

In this section, we give an explicit combinatorial formula for the ee-coefficients of J(n)​(x,q,t)J_{(n)}(x;q,t). We give two proofs of this formula. We first define a weight of a composition with respect to a one-row partition.

Definition 3.1.

For a composition α=(α1,…,αk)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k}) of nn, let

In this subsection, we prove (3.4) by comparing monomial coefficients on both sides using the Haglund–Haiman–Loehr formula (2.5).

For the one-row partition μ=(n)\mu=(n), we can identify each superfilling of μ′=(1n)\mu^{\prime}=(1^{n}) with its reading word. 3.2. Recursive proof

In this subsection, we give a recursive proof of (3.4). We first recall the generating function of J(n)​(x,q,t)J_{(n)}(x;q,t).

We have

=(−1)k−1​(1−qn−k​tk)​(q,q)n−1(q,q)n−k​wt(n−k)⁡(β).\displaystyle=(-1)^{k-1}(1-q^{n-k}t^{k})\frac{(q;q)_{n-1}}{(q;q)_{n-k}}\operatorname{wt}_{(n-k)}(\beta).

4. Hook case

In this section, we give an ee-expansion of Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) when μ\mu is a hook using the one-row case in Section 3. As a consequence, we prove Conjecture 1.1 in this case.

4.1. Main formula

We first extend the definition of the weight wt(n)⁡(α)\operatorname{wt}_{(n)}(\alpha) given in the previous section. Recall that χ⁡(P)=1\chi(P)=1 if PP holds and χ⁡(P)=0\chi(P)=0 otherwise.

Definition 4.1.

For a hook μ=(r,1s)\mu=(r,1^{s}) with r≥1r\geq 1, s≥0s\geq 0, and r+s=nr+s=n, and a composition α=(α1,…,αk)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k}) of nn, define

(4.1) wt(r,1s)⁡(α)=χ⁡(αk>s)​(t,t)s​∏i=1rwt⁡(i,α).\operatorname{wt}_{(r,1^{s})}(\alpha)=\chi(\alpha_{k}>s)(t;t)_{s}\prod_{i=1}^{r}\operatorname{wt}(i,\alpha).

The ee-coefficients of J(r,1s)​(x,q,t)J_{(r,1^{s})}(x;q,t) have a combinatorial description in terms of these weights, as follows.

Theorem 4.2.

Let n,r≥1n,r\geq 1 and s≥0s\geq 0 be integers with r+s=nr+s=n. Then we have

(4.2) J(r,1s)​(x,q,t)=∑λ⊢n(∑α∼λwt(r,1s)⁡(α))​eλ,J_{(r,1^{s})}(x;q,t)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}\left(\sum_{\alpha\sim\lambda}\operatorname{wt}_{(r,1^{s})}(\alpha)\right)e_{\lambda},

where the second sum is over all compositions α\alpha with α∼λ\alpha\sim\lambda.

This theorem will be proved in the next subsection. In what follows, we provide an equivalent description of (4.2) using ribbon tilings.

A ribbon is a connected skew shape containing no 2×22\times 2 block. The content of a cell (i,j)(i,j) is j−ij-i, and the head of a ribbon is its cell of smallest content.

A ribbon tiling of a partition ν\nu is a tiling of its diagram by ribbons. Its type is the partition formed by the ribbon sizes. Write RT⁡(ν)\operatorname{RT}(\nu) for the set of ribbon tilings of ν\nu, and RT⁡(ν,λ)\operatorname{RT}(\nu,\lambda) for those of type λ\lambda. A ribbon tiling is special if each ribbon contains a cell in the first column of ν\nu. Denote the corresponding sets by SRT⁡(ν)\operatorname{SRT}(\nu) and SRT⁡(ν,λ)\operatorname{SRT}(\nu,\lambda).

For T∈RT⁡(ν)T\in\operatorname{RT}(\nu), define

wt⁡(T)=∏c∈νwt⁡(c,T,ν),wt⁡(c,T,ν)={1−qleg⁡(c)​t|θ|,if c is the head of a ribbon θ∈T,qleg⁡(c)−tarm′⁡(c),otherwise.\operatorname{wt}(T)=\prod_{c\in\nu}\operatorname{wt}(c,T,\nu),\qquad\operatorname{wt}(c,T,\nu)=\begin{cases}1-q^{\operatorname{leg}(c)}t^{|\theta|},&\text{if $c$ is the head of a ribbon $\theta\in T$},\\ q^{\operatorname{leg}(c)}-t^{\operatorname{arm}^{\prime}(c)},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Here the leg and coarm lengths are measured in ν\nu.

Theorem 4.3.

Let μ=(r,1s)\mu=(r,1^{s}), where r≥1r\geq 1, s≥0s\geq 0, and r+s=nr+s=n. Then

(4.3) Jμ​(x,q,t)=∑λ⊢n(∑T∈SRT⁡(μ′,λ)wt⁡(T))​eλ.J_{\mu}(x;q,t)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}\left(\sum_{T\in\operatorname{SRT}(\mu^{\prime},\lambda)}\operatorname{wt}(T)\right)e_{\lambda}.

This follows directly from Theorem 4.2 by interpreting each composition with nonzero weight as a special ribbon tiling of μ′\mu^{\prime} with the same weight.

4.2. Proof of Theorem 4.2

Let

(4.4) Y(r,1s)=Y(r,1s)​(x,q,t)=∑α⊨nwt(r,1s)⁡(α)​eα.Y_{(r,1^{s})}=Y_{(r,1^{s})}(x;q,t)=\sum_{\alpha\vDash n}\operatorname{wt}_{(r,1^{s})}(\alpha)e_{\alpha}.

Then Theorem 4.2 is equivalent to

(4.5) J(r,1s)​(x,q,t)=Y(r,1s)​(x,q,t).J_{(r,1^{s})}(x;q,t)=Y_{(r,1^{s})}(x;q,t).

It is known [15, p. 363] that for r,s≥1r,s\geq 1,

(4.6) (1−qr​ts)​J(r)​J(1s)=(1−ts)​J(r+1,1s−1)+(1−qr)​J(r,1s).(1-q^{r}t^{s})J_{(r)}J_{(1^{s})}=(1-t^{s})J_{\left(r+1,1^{s-1}\right)}+(1-q^{r})J_{\left(r,1^{s}\right)}.

We will show that Y(r,1s)​(x,q,t)Y_{(r,1^{s})}(x;q,t) satisfies the same recurrence relation and initial conditions. Note that if (r,1s)=(1,1n−1)=(1n)(r,1^{s})=(1,1^{n-1})=(1^{n}), then by definition we have wt(1,1n−1)⁡(α)=0\operatorname{wt}_{(1,1^{n-1})}(\alpha)=0 unless α=(n)\alpha=(n). Thus,

(4.7) Y(1n)=(t,t)n​en.Y_{(1^{n})}=(t;t)_{n}e_{n}.
Lemma 4.4.

For integers r,s≥1r,s\geq 1, we have

(4.8) (1−qr​ts)​Y(r)​Y(1s)=(1−ts)​Y(r+1,1s−1)+(1−qr)​Y(r,1s).(1-q^{r}t^{s})Y_{(r)}Y_{(1^{s})}=(1-t^{s})Y_{\left(r+1,1^{s-1}\right)}+(1-q^{r})Y_{\left(r,1^{s}\right)}.
Proof.

Let n=r+sn=r+s. By (4.4), the right-hand side of (4.8) is equal to

(4.9) ∑α⊨n((1−ts)​wt(r+1,1s−1)⁡(α)+(1−qr)​wt(r,1s)⁡(α))​eα.\sum_{\alpha\vDash n}\left((1-t^{s})\operatorname{wt}_{(r+1,1^{s-1})}(\alpha)+(1-q^{r})\operatorname{wt}_{(r,1^{s})}(\alpha)\right)e_{\alpha}.

Fix α=(α1,…,αk)⊨n\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k})\vDash n. If αk≤s−1\alpha_{k}\leq s-1, then both weights in (4.9) vanish. If αk≥s+1\alpha_{k}\geq s+1, then r>α1+⋯+αk−1r>\alpha_{1}+\cdots+\alpha_{k-1}, so wt⁡(r+1,α)=qr−1\operatorname{wt}(r+1,\alpha)=q^{r}-1. Hence, the summand in (4.9) also vanishes:

(1−ts)​wt(r+1,1s−1)⁡(α)+(1−qr)​wt(r,1s)⁡(α)=(t,t)s​((qr−1)+(1−qr))​∏i=1rwt⁡(i,α)=0.(1-t^{s})\operatorname{wt}_{(r+1,1^{s-1})}(\alpha)+(1-q^{r})\operatorname{wt}_{(r,1^{s})}(\alpha)=(t;t)_{s}\bigl((q^{r}-1)+(1-q^{r})\bigr)\prod_{i=1}^{r}\operatorname{wt}(i,\alpha)=0.

Therefore, we can restrict the sum in (4.9) to the compositions with αk=s\alpha_{k}=s.

Suppose α=(β,s)\alpha=(\beta,s) with β⊨r\beta\vDash r. Then wt(r,1s)⁡(α)=0\operatorname{wt}_{(r,1^{s})}(\alpha)=0 and

(1−ts)​wt(r+1,1s−1)⁡(α)=(1−qr​ts)​(t,t)s​wt(r)⁡(β).(1-t^{s})\operatorname{wt}_{(r+1,1^{s-1})}(\alpha)=(1-q^{r}t^{s})(t;t)_{s}\operatorname{wt}_{(r)}(\beta).

This, together with eα=eβ​ese_{\alpha}=e_{\beta}e_{s} and (4.7), implies that (4.9) is equal to

(1−qr​ts)​(t,t)s​es​∑β⊨rwt(r)⁡(β)​eβ=(1−qr​ts)​Y(1s)​Y(r).(1-q^{r}t^{s})(t;t)_{s}e_{s}\sum_{\beta\vDash r}\operatorname{wt}_{(r)}(\beta)e_{\beta}=(1-q^{r}t^{s})Y_{(1^{s})}Y_{(r)}.

Now we are ready to prove Theorem 4.2.

Proof of Theorem 4.2.

By Theorem 3.3, we have

J(k)​(x,q,t)=Y(k)​(x,q,t)for all ​k≥1.J_{(k)}(x;q,t)=Y_{(k)}(x;q,t)\qquad\text{for all }k\geq 1.

By [15, p. 339] and (4.7), we have

J(1k)​(x,q,t)=(t,t)k​ek=Y(1k)​(x,q,t)for all ​k≥1.J_{(1^{k})}(x;q,t)=(t;t)_{k}e_{k}=Y_{(1^{k})}(x;q,t)\qquad\text{for all }k\geq 1.

Thus, using (4.6), (4.8), and the above results, we obtain (4.5) by induction on ss. ∎

In this subsection we prove the ee-positivity in Conjecture 1.1 when μ\mu is a hook.

Let μ=(r,1s)\mu=(r,1^{s}) with n=r+sn=r+s, and fix an integer k≥1k\geq 1. For a composition α=(α1,…,αℓ)⊨n\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{\ell})\vDash n and 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r, define

Since the summand is antisymmetric in d0d_{0} and dkd_{k}, the sum over nonnegative integers did_{i} satisfying both d0>sd_{0}>s and dk>sd_{k}>s vanishes. Thus, we obtain

Br,sCs​[r−1]q!\displaystyle\frac{B_{r,s}}{C_{s}[r-1]_{q}!} =∑d0+⋯+dk=ndk≤s<d0qk​d0−qk​dkq−1​q∑i=0k−1i​di​∏i=0kedi\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d_{0}+\cdots+d_{k}=n\\ d_{k}\leq s<d_{0}\end{subarray}}\frac{q^{kd_{0}}-q^{kd_{k}}}{q-1}q^{\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}id_{i}}\prod_{i=0}^{k}e_{d_{i}}
=∑d0+⋯+dk=ndk≤s<d0qk​dk​[k⁡(d0−dk)]q​q∑i=0k−1i​di​∏i=0kedi,\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d_{0}+\cdots+d_{k}=n\\ d_{k}\leq s<d_{0}\end{subarray}}q^{kd_{k}}[k(d_{0}-d_{k})]_{q}q^{\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}id_{i}}\prod_{i=0}^{k}e_{d_{i}},

which is the desired formula. ∎

5. Two-column case

In this section, we provide a formula for the ee-coefficients of Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) and prove Conjecture 1.1 when μ\mu consists of two columns. In this case, each nonzero ee-coefficient of Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) admits a factorization into |μ||\mu| factors.

Theorem 5.1.

Let 0≤ℓ≤⌊n/2⌋0\leq\ell\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor and μ=(2ℓ,1n−2​ℓ)\mu=(2^{\ell},1^{n-2\ell}). Then we have

(5.1) Jμ​(x,q,t)=∑p=0ℓ(qℓ−p​(1−tn−2​p)​(t,t)n−ℓ−p−1​(q−1,t)ℓ−p​(t,t)ℓ(t,t)ℓ−p​(q​t,t)n−ℓ(q​t,t)n−ℓ−p)​e(n−p,p),J_{\mu}(x;q,t)=\sum_{p=0}^{\ell}\left(q^{\ell-p}(1-t^{n-2p})(t;t)_{n-\ell-p-1}(q^{-1};t)_{\ell-p}\frac{(t;t)_{\ell}}{(t;t)_{\ell-p}}\frac{(qt;t)_{n-\ell}}{(qt;t)_{n-\ell-p}}\right)e_{(n-p,p)},

where we use the convention that (1−tn−2​p)​(t,t)n−ℓ−p−1=(t,t)n−2​p(1-t^{n-2p})(t;t)_{n-\ell-p-1}=(t;t)_{n-2p} when p=ℓp=\ell.

Equivalently, we have

Jμ​(x,q,t)=∑p=0ℓ(∏c∈μwtμ,p⁡(c))​e(n−p,p),J_{\mu}(x;q,t)=\sum_{p=0}^{\ell}\left(\prod_{c\in\mu}\operatorname{wt}_{\mu,p}(c)\right)e_{(n-p,p)},

where the weight wtμ,p⁡(c)\operatorname{wt}_{\mu,p}(c) of a cell c=(i,j)∈μc=(i,j)\in\mu is defined by

wtμ,p⁡(c)={1−qarm⁡(c)​tleg⁡(c)+1,if i≤p,1−tn−2​p,if c=(p+1,1),qj−1−ti−p−1,if i>p and c≠(p+1,1),\operatorname{wt}_{\mu,p}(c)=\begin{cases}1-q^{\operatorname{arm}(c)}t^{\operatorname{leg}(c)+1},&\mbox{if $i\leq p$},\\ 1-t^{n-2p},&\mbox{if $c=(p+1,1)$},\\ q^{j-1}-t^{i-p-1},&\mbox{if $i>p$ and $c\neq(p+1,1)$},\end{cases}

with arm and leg lengths measured in μ\mu. See Figure 3.

To prove Theorem 5.1, we use the following lemma.

Lemma 5.2.

For a≥ba\geq b with n=a+bn=a+b, we have

(5.2) ea⋅eb=∑j=0b(q,t)a−j​(q,t)b−j​(1−q​tn−2​j)(t,t)a−j​(t,t)b−j​(t,t)j​(q,t)n−j+1​J(2j,1n−2​j)​(x,q,t).e_{a}\cdot e_{b}=\sum_{j=0}^{b}\frac{(q;t)_{a-j}(q;t)_{b-j}(1-qt^{n-2j})}{(t;t)_{a-j}(t;t)_{b-j}(t;t)_{j}(q;t)_{n-j+1}}J_{(2^{j},1^{n-2j})}(x;q,t).

Using Theorem 5.1, we can prove Conjecture 1.1 when μ\mu has at most two columns.

For every partition μ\mu with at most two columns and every positive integer kk, the expression in (1.5) has ee-coefficients in ℤ≥0​[q]\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}[q].

6. The ene_{n}-coefficient

Combining the relation between Pμ​(x,q,t)P_{\mu}(x;q,t) and Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) with the triangularity of Pμ​(x,q,t)P_{\mu}(x;q,t) in the monomial symmetric function basis, we obtain

Jμ​(x,q,t)=∑λ≥μ′cμ,λ​eλ,J_{\mu}(x;q,t)=\sum_{\lambda\geq\mu^{\prime}}c_{\mu,\lambda}e_{\lambda},

where

(6.1) cμ,μ′=∏c∈μ(1−qarm⁡(c)​tleg⁡(c)+1)=∏c∈μ′(1−qleg⁡(c)​tarm⁡(c)+1).c_{\mu,\mu^{\prime}}=\prod_{c\in\mu}(1-q^{\operatorname{arm}(c)}t^{\operatorname{leg}(c)+1})=\prod_{c\in\mu^{\prime}}(1-q^{\operatorname{leg}(c)}t^{\operatorname{arm}(c)+1}).

In particular,

J(1n)​(x,q,t)=(t,t)n​en.J_{(1^{n})}(x;q,t)=(t;t)_{n}e_{n}.

More generally, we compute the ene_{n}-coefficient of Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) for any μ⊢n\mu\vdash n.

Theorem 6.1.

For n≥1n\geq 1 and μ⊢n\mu\vdash n, we have

[en]​Jμ​(x,q,t)\displaystyle[e_{n}]J_{\mu}(x;q,t) =(1−tn)(q−1)⋯(qμ1−1−1)∏c∉Row1⁡(μ)(qarm′⁡(c)−tleg′⁡(c))\displaystyle=(1-t^{n})(q-1)\cdots(q^{\mu_{1}-1}-1)\prod_{c\notin\operatorname{Row}_{1}(\mu)}(q^{\operatorname{arm}^{\prime}(c)}-t^{\operatorname{leg}^{\prime}(c)})
=(1−tn)(q−1)⋯(qμ1−1−1)∏c∉Col1⁡(μ′)(qleg′⁡(c)−tarm′⁡(c)),\displaystyle=(1-t^{n})(q-1)\cdots(q^{\mu_{1}-1}-1)\prod_{c\notin\operatorname{Col}_{1}(\mu^{\prime})}(q^{\operatorname{leg}^{\prime}(c)}-t^{\operatorname{arm}^{\prime}(c)}),

where Row1⁡(μ)\operatorname{Row}_{1}(\mu) (resp. Col1⁡(μ)\operatorname{Col}_{1}(\mu)) is the set of cells in the first row (resp. column) of μ\mu. Equivalently,

(6.2) [en]​Jμ​(x,q,t)=(1−tn)​∏c∈μ′∖{(1,1)}(qleg′⁡(c)−tarm′⁡(c)).[e_{n}]J_{\mu}(x;q,t)=(1-t^{n})\prod_{c\in\mu^{\prime}\setminus\{(1,1)\}}(q^{\operatorname{leg}^{\prime}(c)}-t^{\operatorname{arm}^{\prime}(c)}).

To prove Theorem 6.1, we need the following lemma.

Lemma 6.2.

Let n≥1n\geq 1. If

f=∑λ⊢naλ​eλ,f=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}a_{\lambda}e_{\lambda},

then

(6.3) [en]​f=(−1)n−1​(1−tn)​limu→1f⁡[1−u1−t]/(1−u).[e_{n}]f=(-1)^{n-1}(1-t^{n})\lim_{u\to 1}f\left[\frac{1-u}{1-t}\right]/(1-u).
Proof.

(6.4) em​[1−u1−t]=∑λ⊢m(−1)m−ℓ⁡(λ)​zλ−1​pλ​[1−u1−t],e_{m}\left[\frac{1-u}{1-t}\right]=\sum_{\lambda\vdash m}(-1)^{m-\ell(\lambda)}z_{\lambda}^{-1}p_{\lambda}\left[\frac{1-u}{1-t}\right],

=a(n)​(−1)n−1​1−u1−tn+O⁡((1−u)2).\displaystyle=a_{(n)}(-1)^{n-1}\frac{1-u}{1-t^{n}}+O((1-u)^{2}).

Then the result follows by taking the limit as uu approaches 11 and solving for the coefficient a(n)a_{(n)}. ∎

Proof of Theorem 6.1.

By [15, Ch. VI, (8.8)], we have

Jμ​[1−u1−t;q,t]=∏c∈μ(tleg′⁡(c)−qarm′⁡(c)​u).J_{\mu}\left[\frac{1-u}{1-t};q,t\right]=\prod_{c\in\mu}\left(t^{\operatorname{leg}^{\prime}(c)}-q^{\operatorname{arm}^{\prime}(c)}u\right).

Since all cells in the first row have coleg length 00, we obtain the first identity. The remaining expressions follow directly from analyzing the diagram of μ\mu. ∎

7. Final remarks

In this section, we explain the analogy between the normalization of Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) in Conjecture 1.1 and the α\alpha-chromatic symmetric functions introduced by Haglund, Oh, and Yoo [9]. We then propose a conjecture on an expansion of the normalized Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) in terms of chromatic symmetric functions when q=1q=1.

For a graph GG with vertex set V={v1,…,vn}V=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\}, the chromatic symmetric function χG​(x)\chi_{G}(x) is defined by

χG(x)=∑c:V→ℤ+xc⁡(v1)⋯xc⁡(vn),\chi_{G}(x)=\sum_{c:V\to\mathbb{Z}^{+}}x_{c(v_{1})}\cdots x_{c(v_{n})},

where the sum is over all proper colorings cc of GG. If GG is the incomparability graph of a natural unit interval order, then it can be identified with a Dyck path γ\gamma of length 2​n2n. From now on, we consider only such graphs and write χγ​(x)\chi_{\gamma}(x) in place of χG​(x)\chi_{G}(x). See [18, 9] for more details.

By (1.4), the normalization of Jμ​(x,q,t)J_{\mu}(x;q,t) in Conjecture 1.1 satisfies

qk​∑i≥1i​μi​Jμ​(x,q,q−k)(q−1)n=H~μ​[(qk−1)​X;q,qk](q−1)n.q^{k\sum_{i\geq 1}i\mu_{i}}\frac{J_{\mu}(x;q,q^{-k})}{(q-1)^{n}}=\frac{\tilde{H}_{\mu}[(q^{k}-1)X;q,q^{k}]}{(q-1)^{n}}.

Applying the same plethystic substitution to the unicellular LLT polynomial LLTγ⁡(x,q)\operatorname{LLT}_{\gamma}(x;q) and dividing by (q−1)n(q-1)^{n} gives the α\alpha-chromatic symmetric function at α=k\alpha=k:

χγ(k)​(x,q)=LLTγ⁡[(qk−1)​X;q](q−1)n.\chi_{\gamma}^{(k)}(x;q)=\frac{\operatorname{LLT}_{\gamma}[(q^{k}-1)X;q]}{(q-1)^{n}}.

When q=1q=1, the α\alpha-chromatic symmetric functions are polynomials in α\alpha whose coefficients are symmetric functions. Hence, they can be expanded in terms of the basis {(αr)}r≥0\{\binom{\alpha}{r}\}_{r\geq 0} of the polynomials in α\alpha. Haglund, Oh, and Yoo [9, Theorem 4.4] showed that each coefficient of (αr)\binom{\alpha}{r} has a positive expansion in terms of chromatic symmetric functions:

(7.1) χγ(α)​(x,1)=∑r=1n(αr)​r!​∑S∈𝒮⁡(n,r)χβ⁡(γ,S)​(x).\chi_{\gamma}^{(\alpha)}(x;1)=\sum_{r=1}^{n}\binom{\alpha}{r}r!\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}(n,r)}\chi_{\beta(\gamma,S)}(x).

Here 𝒮⁡(n,r)\mathcal{S}(n,r) denotes the set of all set partitions of {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dots,n\} into rr blocks, and β⁡(γ,S)\beta(\gamma,S) is a certain Dyck path determined by γ\gamma and SS. By Hikita’s theorem [12], this implies that χγ(α)​(x,1)\chi_{\gamma}^{(\alpha)}(x;1) is ee-positive for every positive integer α\alpha.

Now we define

J^μ(α)​(x)=limq→1Jμ​(x,q,q−α)(q−1)|μ|.\hat{J}^{(\alpha)}_{\mu}(x)=\lim_{q\rightarrow 1}\frac{J_{\mu}(x;q,q^{-\alpha})}{(q-1)^{|\mu|}}.

Using the Haglund–Haiman–Loehr formula [8, Proposition 8.1], one can see that this is also a polynomial in α\alpha. Inspired by (7.1), we propose the following question.

Question 7.1.

Let n,rn,r be positive integers, μ⊢n\mu\vdash n and 0≤r≤n0\leq r\leq n. Denote by 𝒪​𝒫​(n,r)\mathcal{OP}(n,r) the set of ordered set partitions of {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dots,n\} into rr blocks. For each S∈𝒪​𝒫​(n,r)S\in\mathcal{OP}(n,r), can we find a Dyck path π⁡(μ,S)\pi(\mu,S) such that

(7.2) J^μ(α)​(x)=∑r=1n(αr)​∑S∈𝒪​𝒫​(n,r)χπ⁡(μ,S)​(x)​?\hat{J}^{(\alpha)}_{\mu}(x)=\sum_{r=1}^{n}\binom{\alpha}{r}\sum_{S\in\mathcal{OP}(n,r)}\chi_{\pi(\mu,S)}(x)\ ?

Again by the result of Hikita [12], an affirmative answer to this question would imply the ee-positivity of J^μ(α)​(x)\hat{J}^{(\alpha)}_{\mu}(x) for every positive integer α\alpha.

We note that the chromatic symmetric functions {χγ​(x)}γ∈𝒟\{\chi_{\gamma}(x)\}_{\gamma\in\mathcal{D}}, where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the set of Dyck paths, do not form a basis of the space of symmetric functions. Thus, an expansion of the form (7.2) need not be unique. Note also that if π⁡(μ,S)\pi(\mu,S) depends only on μ\mu and the underlying set partition of SS, then one can rewrite (7.2) as

J^μ(α)​(x)=∑r=1n(αr)​r!​∑S∈𝒮⁡(n,r)χπ⁡(μ,S)​(x),\hat{J}^{(\alpha)}_{\mu}(x)=\sum_{r=1}^{n}\binom{\alpha}{r}r!\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}(n,r)}\chi_{\pi(\mu,S)}(x),

which has the same form as (7.1). However, such a rewriting is not possible in general. For example, if μ=(2,2,1)\mu=(2,2,1), then the coefficient of (α4)\binom{\alpha}{4} has no expansion in terms of chromatic symmetric functions in which every coefficient is a nonnegative integer multiple of 4!4!.
